11197-bambi:
Marjorie Benton Cooke's 1914 novel follows Francesca Parkhurst, called Bambi, the quick-witted daughter of a professor who raised her to be happy without teaching her how to earn a living. When she marries Jarvis, a serious playwright, she sets out to support them both by writing popular stories, clashing with his highbrow ideals and her own ambitions. New York theater life supplies the backdrop.

The novel's charm lies in Bambi's talk: fast, funny, and determined to bend the world to her plans. Beneath the comedy runs a question about marriage and work, as husband and wife negotiate whose art pays the bills. Cooke's best-known book, it captures a moment when women writers were claiming commercial success openly.
16351-critical-and-historical-essays-lec:
Edward MacDowell's Critical and Historical Essays, edited by W. J. Baltzell and published in 1912, shows the composer as a writer on music. In 1896 Columbia University offered MacDowell its newly created chair of music, and he accepted after much thought, becoming one of America's leading composers in a new academic role. His lectures turn from composition to history and aesthetics.

Chapters trace the origin of music and song, the music of Hebrews, Hindus, Egyptians, Assyrians, and Chinese, then Greece, Rome, and the early church. Scale, notation, Hucbald and Guido, counterpoint, instruments, and folk song follow. Music students will find a clear, humane survey from a composer who loved the past.
23213-uncle-wiggily-and-old-mother-hubba:
Howard R. Garis published Uncle Wiggily and Old Mother Hubbard in 1922, a children's book in his long Uncle Wiggily series. The rabbit gentleman at its centre steps into the world of Mother Goose. Its chapter list reads like a roll call of nursery-rhyme figures.

Uncle Wiggily meets Mother Goose herself, then the three little pigs, one by one. He also meets Little Boy Blue, Little Bo-Peep, and Tommie Tucker, among others. Each short chapter gives young readers a fresh small adventure, built from rhymes they may already know by heart.
27975-delineations-of-the-ox-tribe-the-n:
George Vasey published Delineations of the Ox Tribe in London in 1851, with seventy-two wood engravings by the author, dedicated to William Yarrell. The book gives the natural history of bulls, bisons, and buffaloes, exhibiting all known species and remarkable varieties of the genus Bos.

Vasey admits that known facts do not yet allow dividing the genus into sub-genera, and he brings together descriptions of individual specimens with new facts of his own. The frontispiece shows the Sanga or Galla ox of Abyssinia, and the volume is a handsome example of mid-Victorian zoology.
33091-a-volunteer-with-pike-the-true-nar:
Robert Ames Bennet's Volunteer with Pike tells the true narrative of Dr. John Robinson and his love for the fair Señorita Vallois. It was published in Chicago in 1909 with four color illustrations by Charlotte Weber-Ditzler. Its chapters run from the rose in the mire and plain Thomas Jefferson through the president's house and Señorita Alisanda. They go on to gulf and barrier, the web of the plotter, ship and crew, and the hospitable Blennerhassetts. They then turn to the father of waters, General Wilkinson, and the Pawnee peril.

Bennet, author of For the White Christ and Into the Primitive, sets his volunteer beside Zebulon Pike's expedition to the Grand Peak. The author dedicates the journey to his father, who followed after Pike half a century later. It remains a lively historical adventure, grounded in a real expedition and told with the color of its period.
33434-the-squirrels-and-other-animals-or:
George Waring's Squirrels and Other Animals, published in London, illustrates the habits and instincts of many smaller British quadrupeds. It opens with a squirrel waking as spring warmth stirs it from sleep. Its chapters follow foxes, hedgehogs, and other small beasts through their daily lives. Waring writes for young naturalists.

The book's charm lies in its gentle, story-like natural history, where animals speak and act in ways children can follow. Its pictures, including the fox and the hedgehog, add to the delight. For readers who love British wildlife, it is a pleasing, old-fashioned guide to the small creatures of field and wood.
bambi:
Marjorie Benton Cooke published this theatre novel in 1914, illustrated by Mary Greene Blumenschein, and dedicated to Bambi herself, with thanks for being herself. Bambi is no fawn but a vivacious young wife whose husband Jarvis writes plays. The illustrations promise their world: Jarvis before the curtain making a first-night speech, Bambi whirling a joy-bringing letter round the breakfast room.

New York managers, magazines, and money troubles drive the plot. A tale of Bambi's takes the place of honour, illustrated by James Montgomery Flagg, the supreme desire of every young writer. One blunt letter in the middle refuses a friend's protégé and damns his low-grade magazine. Cooke writes a bubbly backstage romance about a wife whose talent may rescue the marriage she adores.
britannica-1911-abitibbi: Abitibbi is the subject of a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, read here inside a shared chunk of text. The entry names a lake and river of Ontario, Canada. The lake, sixty miles long and studded with islands, is shallow, with small timber on its shores. The Hudson's Bay Company once ran its canoe route to the northern fur lands across it. The Grand Trunk Pacific railway now raises its weight. The river runs out rapid for two hundred miles, joining the Moose toward James Bay.
britannica-1911-albi:
One building towers over Albi: the cathedral of Sainte Cecile, a fort-like Gothic church begun in 1277 and finished in 1512. The city of south-west France, capital of the Tarn department, stands forty-eight miles north-east of Toulouse on a branch rail line. It held 14,956 people in 1906 and sits in a strong spot on the left bank of the Tarn. An old bridge and a new one link it to the suburb of La Madeleine.

At the core, tight winding lanes form the old town, ringed by broad streets, with newer parts beyond. The cathedral's bare outer walls set off the carved stone canopy that shades its south door. Within, a rood-screen and choir wall from near 1500 show fine, delicate carving, and paintings of the fifteenth century coat the vaults and walls. Albi is home to an archbishop and a prefect, and its assize court sits there too.
britannica-1911-ashkenazi-sebi: Ṣebi ʾAshkenazi (1656–1718) was a rabbi known as Ḥakham Ṣebi. He served for some time as rabbi of Amsterdam. He resolutely opposed the pseudo-Messiah's followers. Sabbatai Ṣebi was that false messiah. Ashkenazi's independence of character caused a chequered career. He visited many lands during his life. England was among them, and he wielded much influence there. His Responsa, his written legal rulings, are held in high esteem by later scholars of Jewish law.
britannica-1911-biribi:
Biribi, also called Cavagnole, is a French game of chance, banned by law since 1837. It is played on a board marked with the numbers 1 to 70. Players stake money on the numbers they wish to back. The banker holds a bag of cases, each holding a ticket numbered to match the board. He draws a case and calls out its number. The player who backed that number receives sixty-four times his stake.

All other stakes go to the banker, the 1911 Britannica entry notes. The entry is a short note on the game and on a slang use of its name. In the French army, to be sent to Biribi is a cant phrase. It means being sent to the disciplinary battalion in Algeria. The game thus gave its name to a feared military punishment posting. No board picture or rule variants are given in the brief text.
britannica-1911-ephebi:
Ephebi, from Greek words for “those who have reached puberty,” were in Athens and other Greek towns a class of young men from eighteen to twenty. They formed a sort of college under state control. On finishing his seventeenth year the Athenian youth reached his civil majority.

Enrolment made the youth liable to military training, the main object of the Ephebia in its earliest form. He took an oath in the temple of Aglaurus and joined a garrison at Munychia or Acte. After a satisfactory first year the state gave him a spear and shield, with a cloak and broad-brimmed hat. In the second year the ephebi patrolled the frontiers of Attica and at times fought in war. After the 4th century B.C., the entry says, entry stopped being a duty and the college became a kind of university for rich young men.
britannica-1911-farabi:
Fārābī, Abū Nasr Muhammad ibn Tarkhān (about 870–950), was an Arabian philosopher of Turkish stock. He was born at Fārāb in Turkestan and spent his youth there. At Bagdad he learned Arabic and studied mathematics, medicine and philosophy, above all Aristotle. Later he joined the court of the Hamdanid Saif addaula. The prince welcomed him warmly and gave him a small pension. There he lived a quiet, near-ascetic life.

He died at Damascus, having gone there with his patron. His works read clearly, though aphoristic rather than systematic. Avicenna's later fame pushed much of his writing into neglect. His compendium of Aristotle's Rhetoric was printed at Venice in 1484. Dieterici's Leiden editions of his treatises, including the model state, are listed at the close. Two smaller works appear in the Paris opera omnia of 1638.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-council-of-al: Albi's council of 1254, held by St Louis on his return from an unlucky crusade, aimed at stamping out what remained of the Albigensian heresy and reforming clergy and people. Zoen, Bishop of Avignon and papal legate, presided, and its decrees also legislated concerning the Jews. St Louis called the synod while homeward bound, turning from crusade to the ordering of his realm's church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hammurabi:
Hammurabi, sixth king of the first Babylonian dynasty, is known both as a conqueror and as a lawgiver whose code made him famous. His reign's dates are disputed, from about 2130 to about 1950 before Christ. In his thirtieth year he broke Elam's yoke, took Larsa, and called himself King of Sumer and Akkad, knitting north and south Babylonia into one empire.

Letters and chronicles show a ruler busy every year with temples, canals, farming, and justice, in a reign of great literary activity. Scholars link him plausibly with Amraphel of Genesis 14. His Code, cut on a black diorite stele found at Susa in 1901 and now in the Louvre, set his name among antiquity's greatest rulers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-de-albi: Juan de Albi, also called Alba, was a Spanish Carthusian of Val-Christ near Segovia who died on 27 December 1591. Skilled in Eastern languages, above all Hebrew, he was known as a learned commentator on Scripture. His single recorded work, a commentary of notes and selections from both Testaments, appeared at Valencia in 1610 and was reissued at Venice in 1613.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lesbi:
Lesbi was a titular see in Mauretania Sitifensis, suffragan of Sitifis, or Setif, in Algeria. It is not the island of Lesbos, as some state; Lesbos never was a titular bishopric and holds two titular archbishoprics instead, Mytilene and Methymna. All we know of Lesbi comes from the Itinerarium Antonini: it lay twenty-five miles distant from Tupusuctu, or Tiklat, and eighteen miles off Horrea Aninici, now Ain-Roua, south of Bougie.

The town therefore stood on the Sava, that is, the Oued-Bou-Sellam, but no remains are to be seen. Only two of its bishops are recorded: Romanus, a Donatist at the Carthage conference of 411, and Vadius, a Catholic exiled by King Huneric in 484.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-urbi-et-orbi:
Urbi et Orbi, meaning for the city and for the world, marks a papal document addressed not only to Rome but to the whole Catholic world. The phrase belongs especially to the solemn blessing with plenary indulgence which, before Rome's occupation, the pope gave on set occasions from the balcony of the city's chief basilicas. It was imparted yearly at St Peter's on Holy Thursday, Easter, and the feast of Sts Peter and Paul.

It was also given at St John Lateran on the Ascension and at St Mary Major on the Assumption. Extraordinary occasions brought it too, such as a coronation, an enthronement, or a holy year for pilgrims. The entry explains the blessing's form, its indulgences, and its history, including the Ascension blessing. It gives readers a compact guide to one of the papacy's most public rites.
critical-and-historical-essays-lectures-:
Lectures given at Columbia University by the composer Edward MacDowell make up this set of critical and historical essays on music. Scores and pitch tables in the text show how close the talks stay to the notes themselves. Brass instruments get exact, dated treatment.

One talk traces the horn from about 1750 to the valve horn of the late 1800s. The trumpet's crooks and slides, and the trombone as a large trumpet, enter the same account. Folk song is a further theme, in the eleventh lecture. MacDowell writes as a maker of music who also taught it. The book suits readers who want music history told from inside the craft.
doe-osti-3001797-white-paper-scalable-di:
Mike Boyle of Lawrence Livermore pitches a capability in white paper LLNL-TR-2013372, dated November 2025: digital twins that age alongside the machines they mirror. A digital twin couples a physics model to live data from a real part or process, updating itself as the hardware wears. Livermore built part and process level twins for advanced manufacturing, with automated data ingestion and AI calibration around finite element simulation.

Accelerated aging experiments feed the twins, and surrogate models keep the coupled predictions fast enough to use. The white paper's audience is partly the Navy. The framework that watches a printed part degrade could watch a ship's systems, scaling from part to factory floor to fleet. Centralised data infrastructure and modernised workflows are presented as the unglamorous foundations. As a white paper it argues and roadmaps rather than reporting results, setting out a multi year initiative for aging and surveillance.
doe-osti-3017537-2024-international-conf:
Evan Flach of the American Institute of Chemical Engineers wrote this final report, dated February 11, 2026, for award DE-SC0025668. It covers the 2024 International Conference on Microbiome Engineering, held November 12 to 14 at Tufts University in Medford, Massachusetts. The conference linked academic and industry experts working on engineered microbiomes, the communities of microbes that live in soil, factories, food, and the human body.

What set this meeting apart was its engineering frame: design principles applied to microbiomes, not just basic biology. Topics ranged from engineered organisms inside microbiomes to steering communities through nutrients and environment. Energy Department support sent over twenty trainees and early career faculty who could not otherwise have afforded to attend. Session themes crossed synthetic biology, systems biology, microbial ecology, and bioinformatics. The report is a short record of a field deliberately building its shared design language.
doe-osti-3018254-blueprint-stakeholder-s:
Jordan Smart, Myungsoo Jun, and Katherine Amoresano of the National Laboratory of the Rockies, with Erich Feth, Ryan Cryar, and Paul Snyder, wrote this February 2026 guidance, NLR/TP-5T00-96283. It teaches stakeholders how to categorize vulnerabilities in electric vehicle charging systems. A raw vulnerability list does not tell a city, a utility, and a charger maker the same thing; each needs the risk sorted by what they own.

The guidance builds decision points and values for sorting. Exploitation outcomes are one axis. Another is impact: the more severe the technical impact, or the public safety impact, the higher the priority a vulnerability earns at that decision point. Tables lay out the decision outcomes and their descriptions. Read with its companion blueprint, the document gives the charging industry a shared sorting language, so a flaw found in one network gets the same urgency rating everywhere.
doe-osti-3022553-cooperative-agreement-t:
A UCAR closeout report closes the CATALYST cooperative agreement, DOE award DOESC0022070, which ran from 2021 to 2025 under Gerald Meehl. CATALYST studied modes of climate variability. These are the large recurring patterns, such as El Nino and Atlantic multidecadal variability, that drive weather and climate swings on human timescales. The team also studied how well Earth system models predict and reproduce them.

Four research objectives organize the summary. They cover predictability and prediction, interactions between variability modes and model hierarchy, and benchmarking of how modes respond to external forcing including tipping points. High-impact events tied to those modes are the fourth. An appendix lists the E3SM simulations the team ran. The bulk of the report is achievement summaries keyed to a long publication list, from initialized prediction studies to work on inter-basin contrasts in Southern Ocean warming.
doe-osti-3367034-high-burnup-loca-burst-:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/SPR-2026/4610 uses the BISON fuel performance code to ask how readily high-burnup fuel rods burst in a loss-of-coolant accident. Ian Greenquist, Pierre-Clément Simon, Ryan Sweet, and eleven co-authors wrote it. Burst cladding can fragment fuel into fine particles that relocate, a phenomenon regulators scrutinize as plants push fuel to higher burnup. Both pressurized and boiling water reactor cores were modeled.

All once-burned rods in the full-core model were predicted to burst, simplifying the susceptibility accounting across the core's 77 once-burned assemblies. Susceptibility per rod climbs again once burnup passes 70 megawatt-days per kilogram of uranium. Three pulverization models were compared under two criteria sets. The May 2026 analysis gives licensing engineers a map of where high-burnup risk concentrates.
doe-osti-3383524-comparative-analysis-of:
National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-5400-99289, dated July 2026, compares two-wheeled mobility options for the United States Park Police. Shashikiran Peddireddy and Cabell Hodge of the laboratory wrote it with Matthew Cooney of the Park Police itself. The study starts from an overview of how the force's fleet actually operates. It then surveys the two-wheeled options on the market.

A framework chapter sets out how micromobility could be deployed in Park Police operations. It asks which duties suit a small two-wheeled vehicle, and what support it needs. Results and a conclusion follow. The value of the pairing shows in the byline. The laboratory brings vehicle analysis, and the force brings the operational facts about patrol work. Those facts decide whether an option is suitable, not just efficient.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBIDallasFieldO:
Harold Weisberg wrote to Julia Shea on June 11, 1980 about a records fight with the FBI's Dallas field office. Weisberg had filed Privacy Act requests for files the office held. He reports that the office complied only in part and withheld records he believed were his to see.

The letter is a progress report from a long campaign of requests and appeals. Weisberg spent years forcing assassination records out of the Bureau, office by office. Dallas held central files on the Kennedy case, so its refusals mattered. His account to Shea preserves the state of that fight in mid-1980.
nasa-tm-19700032560-erosion-of-a-three-s:
G. M. Kaplan of the Lewis Research Center and E. Schnetzer of the General Electric Company wrote this paper for a 1970 energy conference in Las Vegas. It reports blade erosion in a three-stage potassium vapor turbine. NASA had worked on such turbines since 1961.

An earlier two-stage turbine had run for thousands of hours in tests. A three-stage machine then finished its own long endurance run. Wet potassium vapor can chew at turbine blades over time. The paper reports the erosion found after the long test. Such turbines were candidates for making electricity in space from a nuclear heat source.
podcast-joerogan-P7xu0t9dTbI:
Filmmaker Bart Sibrel joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2141 to make his case that the moon landings were faked. Sibrel has spent decades on the claim, confronting astronauts and building films around the footage he calls staged. Rogan gives the skeptic a full hearing.

Sibrel lays out his best points, from flag movement to radiation belts, and tells of his run-ins with the Apollo crew. Rogan tests the arguments and asks what proof would change Sibrel's mind. The episode preserves the moon-hoax case in its most committed form, useful for anyone who wants to hear it whole before judging it.
podcast-tuckercarlson-orgvAk7JhBI:
Professor Dave Collum joins Tucker Carlson for a year-end style talk that roams very wide. The title names a financial crisis, Diddy, energy weapons, QAnon, and the deep state's shift to digital tools. Collum teaches chemistry and talks markets on the side.

Collum gives his blunt read on debt, banks, and the risk of a crash. He then roams into crime tales, secret tech, and the tales that swirl online. Carlson lets him range and jumps in with his own takes. Listeners get a free-wheeling talk with a sharp, funny guest. The library holds it as a record of the chat.
